analysis.one_liner: Bans internet and mail-order tobacco sales by treating them as illegal imports and letting states sue.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would shut down the remote sale of tobacco: any cigarettes or smokeless tobacco ordered by phone, mail, or the internet, or shipped by a delivery service, would lose the personal-use exemption from import rules, meaning ordinary shipments would face seizure and civil penalties. States would gain access to Customs records, the power to seize illegal tobacco found in their territory, and the right to sue violators. Companies holding federal tobacco permits could also sue to stop delivery-sale importers, and smokeless tobacco would face the same entry rules as cigarettes.
analysis.who_benefits: State governments would benefit through better collection of tobacco excise taxes, since the bill is aimed at the channel smokers used to buy tobacco without paying state taxes. Licensed tobacco manufacturers, importers, and distributors would gain a protected market, because the bill hands them legal standing to sue competitors operating through the delivery-sale channel. Supporters also cited enforcement against tobacco sold to minors and in violation of import law.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State tax collectors and licensed tobacco sellers

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'delivery sale' as any tobacco purchase made by phone, mail, or the internet, or shipped by common carrier, and strips such sales of the personal-use exemption from tobacco import requirements [S2][S3].

Gives states, through their attorneys general, access to Customs Service certifications for cigarette imports and the right to bring civil actions for civil penalties, damages, and injunctions against violators [S2][S3].

Allows any business holding a federal tobacco permit to sue in federal court to prevent and restrain violations, effectively making licensed tobacco firms private enforcers against unlicensed or remote sellers [S2][S3].
Extends the same entry requirements and enforcement mechanisms to smokeless tobacco products, and allows tobacco found in violation to be forfeited to any state for destruction [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Adult smokers, especially those in states with high tobacco taxes, would lose a cheaper, legal way to buy tobacco and would pay more at retail. Internet, mail-order, and tribal tobacco sellers would lose their business model. Package carriers would have to police or refuse tobacco shipments.

drawbacks.text: The bill's central effect is to close the discount channel: by removing the personal-use exemption and imposing civil penalties for relanded delivery-sale tobacco, it would make ordinary mail shipments of remotely ordered tobacco illegal, raising what smokers in high-tax states pay [S2][S3].

It grants litigation power to tobacco permit holders, allowing companies that sell tobacco commercially to sue competitors, an enforcement mechanism that primarily serves the licensed industry rather than the public [S3].

The enforcement regime relies on forfeiture and seizure, letting states confiscate tobacco found anywhere in their territory for destruction, which applies to otherwise legal products bought for personal use [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real public-interest rationale: stopping tobacco sold to minors and enforcing import and labeling laws. But the bill's main practical effect would be to raise the price of tobacco for adult smokers by cutting off the cheaper mail-order and internet channel, while funneling tax revenue to state governments and handing enforcement power to the licensed tobacco industry. The public-health benefit is genuine but narrow; the price burden and the private-litigation provision fall on consumers and small remote sellers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in November 2005 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Devin Nunes introduced the bill in the House on November 9, 2005 [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tariffs and tobacco tax matters [S5][S3].
No cosponsors signed on, from either party [S4].
No further action was taken before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet, mail-order, and tribal tobacco sellers keep their market, and smokers keep their cheaper buying channel. State governments and the licensed tobacco industry did not get the expanded enforcement and protected market the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Remote and tribal tobacco sellers, and smokers

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or a vote; the bill sat there until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors signed on from either party and no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be determined.

industries.industry: Internet and mail-order tobacco sellers (including tribal smoke shops)
industries.note: The bill defines their entire sales model — orders placed by phone, mail, or internet and shipped by carrier — as a regulated 'delivery sale' stripped of the personal-use import exemption, with civil penalties for relanded product. Their ability to sell cheaply is also what keeps tobacco cheap for consumers, so their interest runs alongside smokers'.

industries.industry: Licensed tobacco manufacturers, importers, and distributors
industries.note: The bill routes enforcement through federal tobacco permit holders, letting licensed firms sue competitors off the market, and locks the remaining legal tobacco trade into the licensed, taxed channel. Their gain comes from eliminating a cheaper alternative that consumers were using.
States would gain seizure rights, access to Customs records, and standing to sue, aimed squarely at the channel used to avoid state tobacco taxes. The revenue comes from prices paid by smokers.
The bill would put carrier-delivered tobacco squarely inside the enforcement regime, forcing carriers to police shipments or refuse tobacco deliveries.
